title: Being held over at the Penn Theater and the big band era
summary: Green says this was the first time he was held over; he rambles on repeat performances, talent scouts, fan clubs, and Whiteman introducing Ellington as King of Jazz.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Well, I think we got held over there, you see. We got held over at this place, see. That's the Penn Theater, see. Now, that's the first experience that I ever had of being held over. Even with Buck and Bubbles, I mean, we wasn't like in no held-over shows, but we had been in the -- you know, like doubling-- like you'd work in one theater and have to go out of that theater and have to go to the other theater and work. They call that doubling, see. Our repeat performance -- because in one city if the same act is going on and on in the same city in different neighborhoods or different parts of a city -- see, that's like repeat performance, you see. Because that's what I say -- popularity, you see, was in great demand. And that's who's the talent scouts -- they send the talent scouts out to observe, to discover these popularities -- the favorites, you know, that was in popularity, see, and that's what happened, you see. They had a protégé -- Mitzi Green -- she was a protégé. And the talent scouts discovered her, see. Of course, they -- the one of a kind thing was what was actually really happening there, you see. Everyone had some kind of style or some of -- there was some kind of modeling they would do. They had a way of -- like Josephine Baker (unintelligible). She had

something. You understand? The way of being outstanding -- getting most of the attention while the performance goes on, you see. Causing the bows, you see. Well, that's what happened. Then, that was something else, so it -- by it happening, --- because Duke Ellington was like a (unintelligible), you know, a Everyone would -- very good ingredient. (unintelligible) most of the fan clubs, wherever he Just to hear you know, was trying to get to where was, see. (unintelligible) they'd you know, Make reservations, you see. The theaters was -- they were very competitive, you know. They tried (unintelligible) that's good box office there, you know, (unintelligible) turn- this, that and the other, They're setting in the aisle and the people are demanding more this, that and the other. "Maybe we should keep them (unintelligible) "Let's see if we can get a breach of contract," or something, you know. Are you following me? I hope you are, because in the future these things will be very important to anyone who has the diplomacy of the way of life, see. Especially this time of the profession. The big band era is coming into -- is beginning to take over, see. They're beginning to have tournaments, you know, and things like that. Like they would have one big band and maybe there'd be two or three other big bands just mingling in the audience and they want to become -- they want to educate themselves. They're wanting to be more to music and to learn and they want to be enraptured by their own abilities, you see. Maybe become great leaders like -- especially Pop, I'll say, Duke Ellington, you see. Even Paul Whiteman in there. He

walked up on the stage and actually told an audience once, you know, he said, -- well, this is really -- Pop says to him, says "Hi. Ladies and gentlemen, this is Duke Ellington. I'm introducing to you the King of Jazz." And they laughed -- the audience. Paul Whiteman -- oh, so naturally, you try to hear yourself think (unintelligible). Everybody -- standing ovation or whatever, you know. It was just -- I mean it was a bedlam, you see, overwhelming -- make the people so happy, you see. Because he had -- he was what we call an Americn find -- a winner you see. He was representing one of our great young men, George Gershwin, you know. Everybody loved his music, you see. But you know what he said? He said, "Thank you very much." And he said, "My host has really -- His Majesty," he said. And then -- so these partialities, I shall say, was enlightening, see. There was a lot of great schools -- student bodies, you know. They would be in the audiences, you see. And these things are very important, you know. The electrical companies and everyone, you know. They was getting proud -- sticking out their chests again, you see. The land of the free and the home of the brave, see.
